title: Closed-loop feedback-feedforward control in flotation bank using peristaltic pumps
author: Quintanilla, Navia, et al.
materials: The experiments were carried out in a two-phase system (water and air) with chemical reagents.

The chemical reagents allowed for a froth layer with sufficient stability to be generated. The feed tank was filled with tap water (from Santiago, Chile), and then the chemical reagents were added in the following order:(1)Methylene blue at a concentration of 10 ppm,(2)Methyl isobutyl carbinol (MIBC) at a concentration of 330 ppm,(3)Frother Flottec F160–10 at a concentration of 20 ppm, and(4)Xanthan gum at a concentration of 600 ppm.

Methylene blue was used to measure air recovery. Air recovery is a measure of froth stability, and it is defined as the fraction of air entering a flotation cell that overflows the cell lip as unburst bubbles [16,17]. To be able to measure air recovery, optical lasers and cameras were placed at the top of each cell, as described in [14]. The optical lasers are used to measure froth height over the cell lip, and the cameras are used to measure the horizontal overflowing froth velocity using image analysis software. The cameras used in these experiments were digital video cameras (commercially available webcams) that were directly connected to the same computer in which the image analysis software was installed. The optical lasers can measure only opaque surfaces, and since this system was two-phase only (i.e. without solids), methylene blue was needed to produce sufficient opaquest between bubbles at the froth surface. Frother and surfactants, such as Flottec 160–10 and MIBC, are commonly added in flotation systems to control bubble size in the pulp phase, as well as to stabilise the froth phase. In addition, a viscosity modifier, such as xanthan gum, is usually used for laboratory-scale experiments without solids. In this study, commercially available xanthan gum was used for all experiments.

The first three reagents (methylene blue, MIBC and frother) were added directly to the feed tank, which was stirred for 5 min to homogenise the mixture. Due to the high thickening property of xanthan gum, it is recommended to prepare the 600-ppm solution in a smaller container (i.e. external to the system), as it tends to form lumps in the beginning. Once the xanthan gum solution is homogeneous, it must be poured into the feed tank and stirred with an external agitator for an additional 5 min. It should be noted that the water used to prepare the xanthan gum solution was also considered in the final mixture. For example, if the feed tank had a capacity of 100 litres, then the tank should initially be filled with 98 L of water (to which the Flottec-160–10 and MIBC were added), and the remaining 2 L of water should be used for the preparation of the xanthan gum solution. Concentrations in ppm of all reagents should be thus based on a total of 100 litres.

steps.title: Prepare Reagent Solutions
steps.instruction: Prepare the chemical reagents for the two-phase (water and air) system, ensuring the xanthan gum is handled separately to avoid lumps.

substeps.instruction: Fill the feed tank with tap water (Santiago, Chile), leaving enough room for the xanthan gum solution (e.g., if the tank capacity is 100 L, fill with 98 L initially).
Add Methylene blue at 10 ppm, Methyl isobutyl carbinol (MIBC) at 330 ppm, and Frother Flottec F160–10 at 20 ppm directly to the feed tank.
Stir the mixture for 5 min to homogenize.
Prepare a 600 ppm xanthan gum solution in a separate smaller container until homogeneous.
Pour the xanthan gum solution into the feed tank and stir with an external agitator for an additional 5 min.
Ensure all reagent concentrations (ppm) are calculated based on the total final volume (e.g., 100 L).

steps.title: Tune Control Parameters
steps.instruction: Determine the initial and final PI control parameters (Kc and τi) for each flotation cell using step changes and trial-and-error.

substeps.instruction: Perform step changes for the peristaltic pumps in triplicates to observe level changes.
Select two points from the level response to calculate Δy and Δt, then calculate k′ using the formula k′ = Δy / (Δt · Δu).
Determine the response time θ graphically (the time when the output level stops changing).
Calculate initial Kc and τi using the assumptions θ = τc and τi = 8θ (ensuring τi ≥ 4(τc + θ)).
Iterate τc and perform trial-and-error experiments implementing a feedback-feedforward strategy to determine the final tuning parameters.

steps.title: Implement Control Strategy in MATLAB
steps.instruction: Codify the control implementation in MATLAB to manage the peristaltic pumps and monitor cell levels.

substeps.instruction: Set the air flowrate to 47 lpm (superficial gas velocity jg = 0.87 cm/s) in each cell for 5 min to reach steady state.
Create setpoint arrays for the level of each cell.
Establish a while loop for the control strategy with a sampling time of 1 second and a total experiment duration of 15 min.
Read optical level sensor signals using ddereq and filter them using a median moving filter (medfilt1) with a window size of 10 s.
Calculate control signals and send them to the peristaltic pumps via ddereq, ensuring manipulated variables stay within the pump's permitted ranges.

steps.title: Validate Control Performance
steps.instruction: Compare the feedback-only and feedback-feedforward control strategies using the Integral Absolute Error (IAE).

substeps.instruction: Apply disturbances to the feed flowrate (Qfeed); for cell 1, maintain a constant 45 lpm, while for cells 2 and 3, use the tailings flowrates from the preceding cells.
Calculate the IAE for each experiment using the formula IAEi = ∫|ei| dt.
Compare the IAE values and the variability of the manipulated variables between the two strategies.
